# A2A and MCP: Complementary Protocols for the Agentic AI Stack

Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) and Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different interoperability problems. MCP standardizes how an LLM application connects to tools, data sources, prompts, and other capabilities; A2A standardizes how independent agents discover one another, delegate work, exchange messages, and track collaborative tasks. In a typical system, MCP operates inside each agent, while A2A connects agents across services, teams, vendors, clouds, or organizations.

A2A’s most important innovations are its Agent Card discovery model, opaque-agent boundary, explicit task lifecycle, long-running-work support, multimodal artifacts, streaming and webhook updates, and multiple protocol bindings. These features address fragmented agent ecosystems and bespoke point-to-point integrations. They do not, by themselves, establish that a remote agent is trustworthy, that its advertised skills are genuine, that its data is semantically consistent, or that a delegated credential is appropriately scoped.

The comparison is also date-sensitive. Google announced A2A on April 9, 2025; version 1.0.0 was officially released on March 12, 2026; and the project later moved through Linux Foundation and Agentic AI Foundation governance milestones. The dated MCP specification available for this comparison is 2026-07-28, whose stateless core differs materially from the stateful 2025-11-25 model still used by some deployed implementations.

## Roadmap

The discussion first establishes A2A’s release history and technical model, then describes MCP using its current and version-specific architecture. It next compares the protocols across their shared dimensions, shows how they work together in one workflow, examines which A2A features are genuinely distinctive and which claims require qualification, and finally maps A2A’s mechanisms to the concrete interoperability and enterprise problems it was designed to address.

## A2A: release context, purpose, and core model

### From Google launch to shared governance

Google introduced A2A at Google Cloud Next on April 9, 2025, describing it as an open protocol for agents built by different vendors and frameworks to communicate, exchange information, and coordinate actions. The launch announcement named more than 50 supporting technology partners, including Atlassian, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, and Workday, although it did not define the denominator or counting method for that figure. [Google’s launch announcement](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/)

The project subsequently moved beyond Google’s direct stewardship. On June 23, 2025, the Linux Foundation announced the Agent2Agent Project as an independent, vendor-neutral open-source project seeded by Google’s transfer of the specification, SDKs, and developer tooling. That announcement reported support from more than 100 companies and named AWS, Cisco, Google, Microsoft, Salesforce, SAP, and ServiceNow among the participants. [Linux Foundation launch announcement](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-launches-the-agent2agent-protocol-project-to-enable-secure-intelligent-communication-between-ai-agents)

The release history that can be established from the supplied evidence is:

| Date | Development | Technical or governance significance | Qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| April 9, 2025 | Google announces A2A | Public launch of the open agent-interoperability protocol | More than 50 partner-support claims were self-reported |
| June 23, 2025 | Linux Foundation launches the Agent2Agent Project | Specification, SDKs, and tooling move toward vendor-neutral governance | The support count exceeded 100 in the announcement but had no defined denominator |
| July 30, 2025 | A2A v0.3.0 | Adds or formalizes gRPC, signed-card support, mTLS and per-skill security fields, OAuth metadata, and the change to `agent-card.json` | The later v1 release introduces breaking interaction changes |
| March 12, 2026 | A2A v1.0.0 | First officially recorded stable release; formalizes the data model, bindings, versioning, signatures, modern OAuth flows, and multi-tenancy | The official GitHub release date is stronger evidence than secondary accounts dating stability to April |
| May 2026 | v1.0.1 is reported in secondary release tracking | Patch-level documentation and specification fixes | The supplied evidence does not include a primary release record resolving every v1.0.1 date detail |
| August 2026 | AAIF governance milestones are reported | A2A is described as joining or becoming hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation | One report gives August 17; the A2A project gives August 27 for Growth Stage acceptance; the evidence does not reconcile whether these are separate milestones |

The early version sequence remains partly unavailable. The supplied material contains a guide describing version 0.2.2, an enterprise page for 0.2.5, and an official listing of previous versions that includes 0.2.6 and 0.3.0. It does not provide one authoritative, timestamped account of the initial 0.2.2-to-0.2.5-to-0.2.6 sequence. That uncertainty matters when reading older tutorials: methods such as `tasks/send`, the older `kind` discriminator, and `/.well-known/agent.json` belong to earlier examples and should not be assumed to describe the v1 wire format.

The official v1.0.0 release records March 12, 2026 and describes the release as breaking relative to v0.3.0. A2A v1 preserves the broad architecture but changes operation names, data representations, version negotiation, Agent Card structure, task-state enum values, and push-notification models. [A2A v1.0.0 release](https://github.com/google/A2A/releases/tag/v1.0.0) [A2A v1 changes](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/whats-new-v1/)

The governance picture also requires careful wording. The Linux Foundation transition in June 2025 is directly documented. A later project announcement dated August 27, 2026 says A2A was accepted as a Growth Stage project at the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), alongside projects such as MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md. A secondary chronology instead reports an August 17 hosted-project announcement and gives AAIF membership counts of 247 organizations from one source and more than 250 from another. These may describe different steps or different counting rules; the supplied evidence does not establish a single authoritative reconciliation. [A2A and AAIF announcement](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/blog/2026/08/27/a-new-chapter-for-a2a-joining-the-agentic-ai-foundation/) [Governance chronology](https://scottarmbruster.com/articles/a2a-agentic-ai-foundation-neutral-agent-standard-2026/)

The practical status by September 13, 2026 is clearer than the exact chronology: A2A has a stable v1 wire model, an open-source project under foundation governance, and a growing set of reported implementations. The adoption figures should still be treated as ecosystem signals rather than audited production measurements. “More than 50 partners,” “more than 100 supporters,” “more than 150 organizations,” “150 organizations in production,” and “247 or 250-plus AAIF members” are not interchangeable populations. They use different denominators and counting rules, and the supplied evidence does not independently measure retention, traffic, task volume, or production depth.

### What A2A is designed to do

The A2A protocol is an application-level standard for communication and interoperability between independent, potentially opaque AI-agent systems. Its goal is to let agents discover capabilities, negotiate supported modalities, manage collaborative work, and exchange information without requiring one agent to inspect the other’s prompts, memory, model, tools, or internal reasoning. [A2A v1 specification](https://github.com/google/A2A/blob/v1.0.1/docs/specification.md)

This is an important distinction from ordinary function calling. A function is usually a capability controlled by the calling application. An A2A remote agent is an independent actor with its own model, policies, tools, state, and operational owner. The caller asks that agent to achieve an outcome; it does not necessarily know how the agent will achieve it.

A2A does not require that agents be owned by different companies. It can be used between services inside one organization. Its strongest motivation, however, is the boundary where the caller does not control the remote implementation: a retailer’s procurement agent communicating with a supplier’s fulfillment agent, a support agent handing a billing dispute to a payment processor, or an orchestrator delegating compliance review to a specialist operated by another team.

### The three-layer architecture

The v1 specification separates A2A into three layers:

1. A canonical data model defines objects such as `Task`, `Message`, `Part`, `Artifact`, `AgentCard`, and extensions.

2. Abstract operations define behaviors such as sending a message, retrieving a task, listing tasks, canceling a task, subscribing to task updates, and retrieving an extended Agent Card.

3. Protocol bindings map those semantics onto JSON-RPC, gRPC, HTTP/REST, or a custom binding.

The project identifies `spec/a2a.proto` as the authoritative normative definition, with generated JSON artifacts and SDK types treated as derived representations. This separation is more than documentation organization. It allows the same task semantics to be represented over different transports while preserving a common contract. [A2A specification architecture](https://github.com/google/A2A/blob/main/docs/specification.md)

### Actors and roles

A2A defines three practical participants:

| Participant | Role |
|---|---|
| User | Human or automated principal whose goal initiates the work |
| A2A Client | Application, service, or agent that formulates requests and acts on behalf of the user or another system |
| A2A Server or remote agent | Agentic system exposing an A2A endpoint, processing tasks, and returning messages, status, or artifacts |

The terms “client” and “server” describe the direction of a particular exchange, not a permanent hierarchy. A remote agent can itself become an A2A client when it delegates a subtask. This role fluidity supports multi-agent chains, but it also means that identity and delegated authorization must be designed across hops rather than assumed from the immediate HTTP connection.

Unlike MCP, A2A has no central Host role that controls all connections and selects all context. The client agent is responsible for deciding when and where to delegate. The remote agent controls its own execution and exposes only the interface it chooses to publish.

### Agent Cards and discovery

An Agent Card is a JSON document describing a remote agent’s identity, endpoint, capabilities, skills, supported modalities, protocol interfaces, authentication requirements, and optional extensions. It functions as a machine-readable service description: the client can determine whether the remote agent appears relevant, which transport and version it supports, and what credentials or capabilities are required before sending a task.

The current v1 discovery convention is:

```text
https://agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json
```

The Agent Card can include:

- human-readable identity and provider information;
- one or more `supportedInterfaces`, each with a URL, protocol binding, and protocol version;
- capabilities such as streaming, push notifications, and authenticated extended-card support;
- supported authentication schemes and required scopes;
- default input and output modes;
- skills with identifiers, descriptions, tags, examples, and input/output modes;
- extension identifiers and whether an extension is required;
- optional tenant information;
- optional signatures.

The v1 design moved the protocol version from the top-level card to each interface. One card can therefore advertise more than one version or binding, allowing a client to select a compatible combination. Clients also send an `A2A-Version` service parameter on requests. Patch versions do not determine wire compatibility; major and minor versions do. [A2A v1 discovery and version changes](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/whats-new-v1/)

Earlier A2A material uses `/.well-known/agent.json`, while the v0.3 and v1-era material uses `/.well-known/agent-card.json`. The supplied evidence does not fully document the compatibility relationship between those paths. Implementers migrating from early versions therefore need an explicit compatibility strategy rather than assuming that every older tutorial and every v1 client use the same endpoint.

Discovery can happen through a well-known URI, a preconfigured URL, or a curated registry. A2A does not prescribe a standard registry API. A registry can add search, ownership, health, freshness, or policy information, but those functions are separate from the core protocol.

The card is an advertisement, not proof that every claim is true. In v1, a card may be signed using JSON Web Signature after JSON Canonicalization Scheme processing. This can protect card integrity and establish provenance when the signer and key are trusted. Signing remains optional, however. A signature confirms who signed the metadata; it does not prove that an advertised skill works correctly, authorize every later task, or authenticate the caller’s subsequent request. [A2A enterprise guidance](https://github.com/google/A2A/blob/main/docs/topics/enterprise-ready.md)

A2A also supports an authenticated extended Agent Card. A public card can advertise `extendedAgentCard`; an authenticated client can then request additional skills or configuration. This permits the server to expose different capabilities to different callers, but it does not replace ordinary authorization checks on task operations.

### Messages, Parts, Tasks, contexts, and artifacts

A2A’s core objects form a small but expressive catalog:

| Object | Main fields or contents | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `Message` | Role, `messageId`, one or more `Part` objects, optional context and task references | A communication turn used to initiate work, ask for clarification, provide input, or report status |
| `Part` | Exactly one of text, inline raw bytes, a URL, or structured data; optional media type, filename, and metadata | Atomic content unit that makes messages and artifacts modality-independent |
| `Task` | Server-generated task ID, optional `contextId`, status, history, artifacts, metadata | Stateful unit of work with a lifecycle and retrievable state |
| `Artifact` | Artifact ID, name, one or more parts, optional extensions | Concrete output of a task, such as a document, image, file, or structured record |
| `AgentCard` | Identity, interfaces, capabilities, skills, security schemes, extensions | Discovery and interaction setup |
| Extension | Versioned URI and optional metadata | Additional functionality negotiated beyond the core protocol |

A `Message` is a turn; it is not necessarily the final deliverable. A client may send a message such as “Review this supplier contract,” and the remote agent may return a `Task`. The task can then produce an artifact containing a compliance report, a structured list of violations, and perhaps a source document.

In v1, `Part` was redesigned as one unified structure. Older versions used separate text, file, and data types with a `kind` discriminator. The v1 representation determines the content type by member presence: `text`, `raw`, `url`, or `data`. A raw part can carry inline base64 bytes; a URL part can reference external content; a data part can carry structured JSON. This is a useful interoperability improvement because the same content model applies to messages and artifacts, but the protocol still depends on implementations to validate URLs, media types, file sizes, and structured data safely.

A `contextId` groups related tasks and messages. It is not itself a complete conversation database or authorization credential. A server may use it to maintain conversational history or LLM context, and a client can use it to continue a related interaction. A `taskId` identifies one stateful unit of work. Task IDs are server-generated for new tasks, while a client can reference an existing task when continuing it.

A completed, failed, canceled, or rejected task cannot be restarted. A refinement normally creates a new task in the same context and may reference the earlier task. This distinction lets an agent preserve task history while treating each new execution as a separate stateful operation. Artifact version linkage is largely a client responsibility: a client that asks for a refinement must decide how the new artifact relates to the earlier one.

### The task lifecycle

A2A has eight task states:

| State | Category | Meaning | Typical client action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED` | In progress | The task has been accepted but has not started active work | Poll, subscribe, or await updates |
| `TASK_STATE_WORKING` | In progress | The remote agent is processing the task | Receive progress or wait |
| `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED` | Interrupted | The agent needs clarification or additional data | Send a follow-up message on the task |
| `TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED` | Interrupted | The agent needs authorization or credentials to continue | Resolve authorization through the agreed external flow |
| `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED` | Terminal | The task finished successfully | Consume artifacts |
| `TASK_STATE_FAILED` | Terminal | Processing ended with an error | Inspect error and decide whether to retry |
| `TASK_STATE_CANCELED` | Terminal | The task was canceled | Start a new task if appropriate |
| `TASK_STATE_REJECTED` | Terminal | The agent refused or could not accept the task | Choose another agent or revise the request |

This state machine is one of A2A’s clearest differences from a simple tool call. It gives a client a common vocabulary for work that may pause, require a person, wait for authorization, or continue after the original connection ends.

The v1 `SendMessage` operation can return a direct `Message` for an immediate response or a `Task` when the work needs tracking. Its execution mode is configurable. With `returnImmediately` unset or false, the operation waits until the task reaches a terminal or interrupted state. With `returnImmediately` true, it returns an in-progress task and leaves the client to retrieve subsequent state using `GetTask`, `SubscribeToTask`, or push notifications. [A2A v1 task behavior](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/whats-new-v1/)

A client can send additional messages while a task remains nonterminal, particularly when the task is waiting for input or authorization. `GetTask` returns current state, artifacts, and optionally history. `ListTasks`, added or formalized in v1, supports filtering and cursor-based pagination, but servers must scope results to tasks visible to the authenticated caller. `CancelTask` requests cancellation; it does not guarantee that work already in progress will stop.

The protocol makes a useful distinction between task state and message delivery. A transient status message may not be persisted in task history, and a disconnected stream may not replay every informational message. Clients should treat artifacts and task snapshots as the reliable business result, not assume that every intermediate message is a durable audit record.

### Synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming interaction

A2A supports three principal delivery patterns.

#### Blocking request and response

For a short task, a client can send one message and receive one completed task or direct message. A purchasing concierge might ask a seller agent to place an order and receive a completed artifact in the response.

“ Synchronous” does not necessarily mean that no task object exists. A remote agent can execute a tracked task and keep the request open until it completes or reaches an interrupted state. The important property is that the caller waits for the result on the current operation.

#### Polling

A client can submit a task without waiting, then call `GetTask` periodically. Polling works across ordinary HTTP infrastructure and is useful when updates are infrequent or the client cannot maintain a persistent connection. Its disadvantages are latency and repeated requests that may return no change.

#### Server-Sent Events

`SendStreamingMessage` establishes an SSE stream. If the remote agent returns a task, the stream begins with the task and then carries ordered status-update and artifact-update events until the task reaches a terminal state. A client can also use `SubscribeToTask` to attach to an existing nonterminal task or reconnect after a broken stream.

Streaming is useful when a remote agent is producing a long report, processing a document in stages, or reporting progress from several downstream systems. The v1 representation uses `statusUpdate` and `artifactUpdate` members instead of the older `kind` discriminator and relies on protocol-specific stream closure rather than a `final` Boolean. Multiple subscribers can observe the same task independently. [A2A streaming guide](https://github.com/google/A2A/blob/main/docs/topics/streaming-and-async.md)

#### Push notifications

For tasks lasting minutes, hours, or days, or for mobile and serverless clients that cannot hold an SSE connection, the client can register an HTTPS webhook. The remote agent sends an HTTP POST containing a task snapshot, message, status update, or artifact update. The client can then call `GetTask` to obtain complete state.

Push is capability-dependent and must be advertised in the Agent Card. A server should validate webhook targets to prevent server-side request forgery, reject private or local addresses where appropriate, authenticate notifications, handle duplicates idempotently, and use replay defenses. These are essential deployment controls; the presence of a push-notification field does not make a webhook safe automatically.

### Transports and protocol bindings

A2A’s v1 specification defines three standard bindings:

- JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP(S);
- gRPC over HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers;
- HTTP+JSON/REST.

SSE carries streaming responses for HTTP-based bindings, while push notifications use HTTP POST even when the original task was initiated over another binding. Custom bindings are possible if they preserve the canonical data model, operations, errors, authentication semantics, event ordering, and capability declarations.

The binding separation is significant for enterprise deployment. A team using conventional REST gateways can expose the HTTP+JSON interface; a service-mesh deployment can use gRPC; a general web application can use JSON-RPC over HTTPS. The specification requires functionally equivalent semantics, but supporting one binding does not automatically mean that an implementation supports all three.

### Authentication, authorization, and enterprise boundaries

A2A treats authentication primarily as an HTTP or transport-layer concern. An Agent Card can declare API keys, HTTP authentication, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, or mutual TLS. The v1 OAuth model adds device-code support for constrained or headless devices, adds a `pkce_required` field to authorization-code flows, and removes implicit and password flows. Credentials are generally acquired out of band and presented in HTTP headers or gRPC metadata. [A2A v1 security changes](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/whats-new-v1/)

Production deployments must use encrypted communication. The exact TLS recommendation is version-sensitive in the supplied guidance, but the invariant is clear: production A2A traffic should use HTTPS or TLS-protected gRPC, certificate validation, secret protection, rate limiting, and normal enterprise identity infrastructure.

After authentication, authorization remains largely agent-specific. A server can authorize by caller identity, skill, scope, tenant, action, data classification, project, or organizational role. v1 supports per-skill security declarations and tenant routing, and it requires task-listing and task-retrieval results to be scoped to the authenticated caller.

The `AUTH_REQUIRED` state is an important coordination mechanism, but it is not itself an authorization grant. The protocol does not define the scope, lifetime, revocation, or downstream binding of the credential obtained in response. A deployment must decide whether a credential authorizes one action, one task, one agent, or a broader session.

Signed Agent Cards are similarly limited. A valid signature can demonstrate that particular metadata was signed by a known key. It does not authenticate later task requests, prove that the caller possesses a particular user delegation, or authorize every skill in the card. The security guidance therefore describes a contract and a set of integration points, not a complete identity and authorization system.

A2A also does not contain a specific protocol control against cross-agent prompt injection. Red Hat’s analysis recommends defense in depth using TLS, trusted-agent policies, authentication, authorization, least privilege, input validation, and monitoring. [Red Hat’s A2A security analysis](https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2025/08/19/how-enhance-agent2agent-security)

### Representative A2A use cases

Google’s launch materials describe a hiring workflow in which a hiring manager’s agent delegates candidate sourcing, interview scheduling, and background-check work to specialist agents. The value is not simply that the agents can exchange text; it is that each specialist can remain independently implemented while exposing a common task interface. [Google’s A2A launch examples](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/)

A Google Cloud walkthrough demonstrates a purchasing concierge built with Google’s Agent Development Kit that discovers two seller agents, one implemented with LangGraph and another with CrewAI. The concierge sends standardized requests to independently deployed services and receives a completed artifact containing an order result. This is an implementation demonstration, not a protocol benchmark, but it illustrates the intended framework boundary. [Google Cloud purchasing walkthrough](https://medium.com/google-cloud/exploring-agent2agent-a2a-protocol-with-purchasing-concierge-use-case-on-cloud-run-36f4b896eadf)

Other representative workflows include contract compliance, where a Python agent extracts terms and a Go agent validates them against policy; employee onboarding across HR, IT, and facilities; supply-chain procurement across retailer and supplier agents; KYC and fraud review; and long-running research or document-generation tasks.

## MCP: purpose, architecture, and core primitives

### What MCP standardizes

The Model Context Protocol was introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 to standardize how LLM applications connect to external tools and data. Its current specification describes MCP as a way for applications to share contextual information with language models, expose tools and capabilities to AI systems, and build composable integrations and workflows. [MCP 2026-07-28 specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28)

The central problem is the repeated integration of models with databases, APIs, filesystems, code execution environments, SaaS systems, and other capabilities. Without a shared interface, every host or agent framework needs a bespoke connector for each external service. MCP reduces that duplication by giving servers a common way to describe and expose capabilities.

MCP is not primarily a protocol for independent agents to negotiate goals. It is a protocol for an LLM application to obtain context and invoke capabilities under the application’s control.

### Host, client, and server

MCP has three roles:

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Host | LLM application that manages the user experience, model interaction, context selection, security policy, and multiple MCP connections |
| Client | Connector inside the host that maintains a connection to one MCP server |
| Server | Process or service exposing tools, resources, prompts, and optional capabilities |

The one-client-to-one-server relationship is an important contrast with A2A’s peer-agent framing. A host can create many clients, one for each server, but each client connection is separately managed. The server does not ordinarily receive the host’s entire conversation. The host selects which context, resource contents, and user information to send.

The host also mediates trust. It decides which servers are available, which tools may be invoked, whether the user must approve an action, and which model context can be shared. A remote MCP server can be operated by another organization, but the MCP architecture still treats it as a capability provider attached to a host rather than as an autonomous peer with its own user-facing task relationship.

### MCP server primitives

MCP’s principal server features are:

| Primitive | Control model | Typical contents | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Resources | Application-controlled | URI-addressed text or binary data, database records, files, API responses | Supplying context selected by the host or application |
| Tools | Model-controlled, normally subject to user approval | Executable functions with names, descriptions, and input schemas | Querying APIs, modifying records, running calculations, executing code |
| Prompts | User-controlled | Reusable prompt templates and guided workflows | Slash commands, structured reviews, domain-specific interaction patterns |
| Sampling | Client-controlled server request | A server asks the host to obtain an LLM completion | A tool or server requests model assistance while the host retains model control |
| Elicitation | Host- and user-mediated | A server requests additional user information | Collecting missing input or confirmation during an operation |
| Roots and logging | Client/server utilities | Accessible directories and structured log messages | Constraining filesystem access and reporting operational events |

Resources are not the same as tools. A resource generally supplies data or context; a tool represents an operation that may have side effects. Tool annotations such as “read-only” or “destructive” are hints and must be treated as untrusted unless the host independently trusts the server.

Prompts also differ from A2A messages. An MCP prompt is a reusable template surfaced to a user or host. It does not represent a remote agent’s stateful task lifecycle. A2A messages, by contrast, are turns inside a collaboration that may result in a task and artifacts.

### Context flow and control

MCP’s context flow is host-mediated:

1. The host decides which server to connect to.
2. The MCP client discovers server capabilities.
3. The host selects resources or makes them available to the model.
4. The model may request a tool through the client.
5. The host applies consent and authorization policy.
6. The server executes the tool and returns structured content.
7. The host decides what result becomes part of the model’s context or user-visible output.

This design keeps the full conversation and user policy at the host. A server typically receives only the data the host chooses to share. It may send notifications, request sampling, or ask for elicitation, but those interactions remain within the host’s control boundary.

MCP therefore standardizes the interface for a capability without requiring the server to be treated as an independent agent. A database MCP server can expose a query tool without claiming to understand the user’s overall goal. A file server can provide resources without negotiating a multi-day workflow with another agent.

### Sessions and version-specific state models

MCP’s session model has changed substantially.

In the 2025-11-25 model, a client sends `initialize` with its supported protocol version, client information, and capabilities. The server replies with its selected version, server information, and capabilities. The client confirms with `initialized`. Remote Streamable HTTP connections can use `Mcp-Session-Id`, and SSE resumability can use event identifiers and `Last-Event-ID`. Capability negotiation and later list-change notifications occur within the initialized connection.

That model is stateful at the protocol layer. It can require sticky routing or shared session storage when a remote server is horizontally scaled.

The 2026-07-28 revision removes the protocol-level session identifier and the initialize/initialized handshake from the new stateless core. Requests carry relevant protocol and client metadata, and capability discovery is performed through the revised discovery model. Applications that need continuity must carry explicit handles such as `job_id`, `browser_id`, or `cart_id` in later tool arguments. [MCP release transition](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28-release-candidate/) [MCP migration guidance](https://aioperator.io/blog/mcp-2026-spec-migration-guide)

Stateless protocol transport does not mean stateless business operations. A server can retain a report job, browser session, shopping cart, or approval case. The difference is that the identifier is explicit and visible to the application rather than hidden in a protocol session. The application must then authorize every use, bind the handle to a principal or tenant, manage expiry and replay, and clean up abandoned state.

A version-aligned comparison must therefore distinguish “MCP” from “the 2025 MCP lifecycle” and “the 2026 MCP lifecycle.” Many guides still describe the former, while new implementations may target the latter.

### Transports

MCP supports two primary transports:

- `stdio`, in which the host launches a local server subprocess and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC over standard input and output;
- Streamable HTTP, in which a local or remote server exposes an HTTP endpoint for client POST requests and optional server-to-client SSE streams.

The older HTTP+SSE arrangement was replaced by Streamable HTTP, although compatibility may remain necessary for existing clients and servers. Stdio relies heavily on process isolation, operating-system credentials, and environment configuration. HTTP deployments require HTTPS, origin validation, authentication, and careful handling of cross-origin requests.

The current 2026 design also adds routing headers, cache hints, and trace-context propagation intended to fit ordinary load balancers and gateways. These changes make it easier to scale stateless MCP HTTP traffic, but they do not remove the need to govern tools, resources, and explicit application state.

### Capability negotiation, extensions, and Tasks

In the 2025 lifecycle, capabilities are negotiated during initialization, and clients commonly discover tools, resources, and prompts through list operations. Servers can notify clients when a list changes.

The 2026 model uses per-request metadata and a formal extension framework. Extensions are opt-in and require explicit support by both sides. Examples include MCP Apps for sandboxed interactive user interfaces and Tasks for asynchronous tool execution.

Tasks should not be confused with A2A’s native task model. In MCP, Tasks are an extension for a tool operation that may outlive a normal request. A tool call can return a task handle, after which the client can poll `tasks/get`, send updates, or request cooperative cancellation. The extension supports long-running work, mid-flight input, and durable handles, but it remains tied to a host’s tool invocation model. It does not create an autonomous peer-agent relationship or provide Agent Card discovery.

### Security and consent

MCP’s current security principles place substantial responsibility on hosts and implementers. Hosts must obtain explicit user consent before exposing user data to servers or invoking tools. Tool descriptions and annotations are untrusted unless the host trusts the server. MCP itself cannot enforce every consent, authorization, privacy, or data-protection principle at the protocol level. [MCP security guidance](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/index)

For HTTP transports, MCP provides a separate authorization framework based on OAuth practices. Stdio implementations normally use the security context of the host process and environment-managed credentials rather than the HTTP authorization flow. The host remains responsible for deciding which server receives which data and which tool calls require confirmation.

MCP’s security boundary is therefore centralized relative to A2A. A compromised or malicious MCP server can still be dangerous, especially if it exposes arbitrary code execution or returns poisoned content, but the host is expected to mediate the connection. A2A assumes that the remote agent may be an autonomous peer outside the client’s control, which creates a different trust problem.

### Typical MCP use cases

MCP is useful when an agent needs to:

- query a database or data warehouse;
- read files or repository content;
- call a web or enterprise API;
- execute code or calculations;
- search a document store;
- retrieve governed resources;
- use a prompt template for a repeatable review;
- request user confirmation or missing information during a tool operation;
- invoke a long-running report, browser, or automation job through the Tasks extension.

A single coding assistant connected to a filesystem and issue tracker may need MCP but not A2A. A multi-agent procurement system may need both.

## Direct differences between A2A and MCP

The shortest accurate comparison is that MCP connects an agent to capabilities it uses, while A2A connects one agent to another agent that performs work. The boundary is architectural rather than absolute: an MCP server can hide an agent-like workflow behind a tool, and an A2A agent can be operated inside one organization. Nevertheless, the protocols make different assumptions about ownership, state, discovery, and trust.

### Side-by-side comparison

| Axis | A2A | MCP | Resulting distinction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary purpose | Coordinate independent agents and delegate tasks | Connect an LLM application to tools, resources, prompts, and context | A2A solves peer coordination; MCP solves capability integration |
| Communicating parties | User, client agent, remote/server agent | Host, client connector, server | A2A exposes an agent boundary; MCP exposes a host-mediated server boundary |
| Agent-to-agent versus agent-to-tool | Agent-to-agent by design | Agent-to-tool or application-to-server by design | A2A treats the remote party as an actor; MCP treats the server as a capability provider |
| Abstraction level | Application-level collaborative workflow | Integration-level context and action interface | A2A carries goals, tasks, status, and artifacts; MCP carries context and tool calls |
| Discovery | Agent Cards, well-known URI, optional registries, direct configuration | Handshake or per-request discovery, list operations, negotiated extensions | A2A discovers who an agent is and what it claims to do; MCP discovers server features |
| Data direction | Bidirectional task conversation and result exchange | Host selects context; server returns data or tool results; server may request sampling or elicitation | A2A supports lateral collaboration; MCP keeps the host in the middle |
| Context direction | `contextId` groups related remote tasks and messages | Host chooses what context or resources the server receives | A2A preserves collaboration continuity; MCP controls context exposure |
| Task handling | Native `Task` object with eight lifecycle states | Ordinary tool calls plus optional Tasks extension | A2A makes long-running collaborative work central; MCP makes it optional |
| State handling | Task state, context IDs, history, artifacts, subscriptions | 2025 sessions; 2026 stateless core with explicit application handles | A2A state is task-oriented; MCP state is version-dependent and increasingly application-visible |
| Synchronous behavior | Direct message or blocking task response | JSON-RPC request/response and tool result | Both support immediate calls, but only A2A’s basic model is a goal-oriented task |
| Asynchronous behavior | Polling, task subscriptions, webhooks, interrupted states | Progress notifications, SSE, and optional Tasks | A2A natively models work that continues after the request |
| Streaming | Ordered task-status and artifact events over SSE; task subscriptions | SSE and notifications over Streamable HTTP; tool progress | A2A streaming has task and artifact semantics; MCP streaming is message transport plus optional task behavior |
| Transports | JSON-RPC/HTTP, gRPC, HTTP+JSON/REST, custom bindings | Stdio and Streamable HTTP, with older HTTP+SSE compatibility | A2A assumes network-distributed agents; MCP also supports local subprocesses |
| Authentication | Card-declared API key, HTTP, OAuth, OIDC, mTLS; credentials out of band | Host/process trust for stdio; HTTP authorization framework and OAuth for remote deployments | A2A advertises cross-boundary requirements; MCP relies more heavily on host mediation |
| Trust boundary | Remote agent is opaque and may be externally operated | Server is normally a subordinate capability provider under host policy | A2A must address peer trust; MCP must protect host consent and tool authorization |
| Extensibility | Card-declared versioned extension URIs and custom bindings | Negotiated extensions such as Tasks and Apps | Both are extensible, but A2A extensions describe peer interaction while MCP extensions describe host-server features |
| Deployment | Cross-service, cross-cloud, or cross-organization HTTP/gRPC | Local or remote, often within one application’s control plane | A2A is most valuable at a real ownership boundary |
| Governance | Google-originated, transferred to Linux Foundation, later reported under AAIF | Anthropic-originated; current specification and release process are community-maintained, with later foundation governance reported in secondary material | A2A’s transition is directly documented; MCP governance details in the supplied evidence are less symmetrical |
| Typical use cases | Supplier handoff, KYC delegation, claims triage, cross-team research, onboarding | Database access, file operations, API calls, code execution, prompts, reports | A2A coordinates specialists; MCP equips each specialist |

### The parties and abstraction level are different

At the wire level, A2A is still a client-server protocol. The “peer” quality comes from what the server represents: an autonomous remote agent rather than a passive function. The client may know only the Agent Card and endpoint, then ask the remote system to achieve an outcome.

MCP’s Host is deliberately more central. A host may manage several MCP clients, select the relevant context, obtain user consent, route messages, and decide which tool result enters the model’s context. Each client is ordinarily connected to one server, and servers are isolated from one another by the host’s connection structure.

This makes A2A the more appropriate abstraction when the remote party owns its own planning, memory, tools, and policies. It makes MCP the more appropriate abstraction when the application owner wants to attach a capability to an agent without exposing or negotiating an independent agent identity.

### Discovery is not the same operation

A2A discovery answers questions such as:

- What kind of agent is this?
- Which skills does it advertise?
- Where is its endpoint?
- Does it support streaming, push, or an extended card?
- Which protocol bindings and versions can it speak?
- Which input and output modes does it claim to accept?
- Which authentication schemes does it require?

MCP discovery answers questions such as:

- Which tools, resources, and prompts does this server expose?
- Which capabilities and extensions does this connection support?
- Has the tool list changed?
- Which request features can this client and server use?

An Agent Card is an externally addressable description of an agent. MCP capability negotiation is normally a connection-level exchange with a server already selected by the host. A2A can use a registry, but the core protocol does not define one. MCP can use a server registry in a host or gateway, but the protocol does not turn servers into autonomous peers.

### A2A’s task state is not equivalent to MCP session state

A2A’s task is a business-level unit of work. It has a lifecycle that can include waiting for input, waiting for authorization, producing artifacts, accepting follow-up messages, and being observed by multiple clients.

MCP’s older session state was primarily protocol state: initialization, negotiated capabilities, notifications, and connection continuity. The current 2026 design removes protocol-level sessions from the core and makes application state explicit through handles. MCP’s Tasks extension adds asynchronous tool execution, but that task is still an operation initiated through the host’s tool interface.

Thus, “both protocols are stateful” is too imprecise. A2A is natively task-stateful. MCP was session-stateful in the 2025 model and is protocol-stateless with application-managed state in the 2026 model, while its Tasks extension adds a separate long-running operation model.

### Streaming means different things

Both protocols can use SSE, but their semantics differ.

A2A defines a stream around a task: an initial task or message, status updates, artifact updates, event ordering, subscription, and closure when the task reaches a terminal state. Push notifications extend this model to disconnected clients.

MCP’s SSE is primarily a way to carry server-to-client JSON-RPC messages or progress over Streamable HTTP. Its core does not define A2A-like artifacts, task states, or peer collaboration. The Tasks extension can supply durable asynchronous execution, but it remains optional and requires explicit support.

### Security assumptions are opposite in emphasis

MCP assumes that the Host can mediate the server connection. Its security guidance emphasizes consent, user control, tool approval, context selection, host policy, and the untrusted nature of tool metadata.

A2A assumes that the client may be delegating to an opaque agent beyond its direct control. It therefore adds discovery metadata, advertised authentication requirements, task visibility, tenant routing, signed-card support, and a cross-service task model. Yet these features do not create a universal trust framework. Authentication is largely transport-layer and implementation-specific; authorization, credential issuance, revocation, provenance, and prompt-injection defense remain deployment responsibilities.

A remote MCP server can cross the same organizational boundary as an A2A agent, so the distinction is not that MCP is always internal and A2A is always external. The distinction is what the protocol means to the application: a remote MCP server is still presented as a capability endpoint, while A2A explicitly represents an independent agent.

## How A2A and MCP work together

The intended composition can be summarized as:

```text
User
  |
  v
Host and orchestrator agent
  | \
  |  \ A2A: discover and delegate to remote agents
  |   \
  |    v
  |  Remote specialist agent
  |       |
  |       +-- MCP --> database, API, filesystem, model, or business tool
  |
  +-- MCP --> orchestrator's own tools and resources
```

The protocols occupy adjacent boundaries:

- MCP moves context and capability access between an agent application and its tools or resources.
- A2A moves tasks, messages, status, and artifacts between independent agents.

### A combined workflow

Consider a KYC onboarding process.

1. A user asks an orchestrator agent to verify a new customer.

2. The orchestrator’s host uses MCP to access its own customer-record resource and obtain the approved onboarding policy. The host decides what user data can be placed into the model context.

3. The orchestrator retrieves the KYC specialist’s Agent Card. The card declares its endpoint, supported input and output modes, authentication requirements, and whether it supports streaming or push updates.

4. After authenticating and applying local policy, the orchestrator sends an A2A `SendMessage` request containing a task such as “Verify this customer under policy version 4,” together with the permitted structured data and any required document parts.

5. The KYC agent’s own host and MCP client connect to an identity-verification MCP server and a credit-check MCP server. The KYC agent chooses which tools to invoke, obtains user or policy approval where needed, and keeps its internal prompts, tool definitions, and memory private.

6. If verification takes time, the KYC agent returns an A2A task in `WORKING`. It may stream status updates, pause in `AUTH_REQUIRED`, or send a webhook when verification completes.

7. The KYC agent returns an A2A artifact containing a verification report, structured risk fields, and references to evidence. The orchestrator can then use MCP to store the report, update a case system, or request human approval.

8. The orchestrator gives the user a result while retaining the A2A task identifier, artifact provenance, and MCP tool-call audit records.

The A2A exchange does not need to know that the KYC agent used MCP. Conversely, the KYC agent does not need to expose its MCP servers to the orchestrator. That opacity is the point: internal implementation can change without changing the external agent contract.

A retail workflow has the same shape. An inventory agent uses MCP to query its warehouse database, then uses A2A to delegate a purchase order to a supplier’s agent. The supplier agent may use MCP to inspect its own inventory and shipping systems before returning an A2A artifact. [Combined A2A/MCP deployment pattern](https://alicelabs.ai/en/insights/a2a-protocol-guide-2026)

### What neither protocol replaces

A2A does not replace MCP for:

- exposing databases, files, APIs, or code execution;
- defining precise tool schemas;
- applying host-mediated consent;
- selecting which local context reaches a model;
- connecting an agent to its own operational systems.

MCP does not replace A2A for:

- discovering independent remote agents;
- advertising agent skills and supported interfaces;
- delegating a goal to an opaque peer;
- tracking a cross-agent task lifecycle;
- receiving task artifacts and status updates;
- handling disconnected multi-party collaboration.

Neither protocol provides a shared enterprise ontology. A2A can carry a field called `revenue`, and MCP can return a correctly typed number, but neither guarantees that two organizations define revenue identically. Neither protocol guarantees data freshness, business-rule consistency, lineage, model quality, or behavioral correctness. [Context-quality limits in A2A and MCP](https://atlan.com/know/mcp/mcp-vs-a2a-protocol/)

Nor does technical reachability grant authorization. A discovered Agent Card is not permission to send confidential data. An MCP tool listed by a server is not permission to invoke it. In a combined system, A2A skill permissions, MCP tool permissions, user identity, tenant scope, delegated tokens, and audit records must align.

### Evidence that the combination is practical

The EMNLP 2025 AgentMaster demonstration implemented both protocols in one modular multi-agent system for multimodal information retrieval, question answering, and image analysis. It reported BERTScore F1 of 96.3% and an LLM-as-a-Judge score of 87.1% in its own pilot evaluation. Those figures describe that framework and its evaluation, not protocol-level guarantees. The paper’s broader point is more relevant here: at the time of writing, relatively few systems had used A2A and MCP together in one multi-agent architecture. [AgentMaster, EMNLP 2025](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-demos.5)

The combination is also reflected in official A2A guidance, which describes an agent using A2A to communicate with other agents while using MCP internally for tools and resources. [A2A and MCP relationship](https://github.com/google/A2A/blob/aca981ce/docs/topics/a2a-and-mcp.md)

## A2A’s innovative design aspects

A2A’s value is best understood as a set of protocol design choices. Terms such as “open,” “secure,” “enterprise-ready,” or “production-ready” are broader claims. The specification defines some concrete mechanisms, but it does not guarantee every outcome implied by those labels.

| Design aspect | What A2A actually specifies | What remains outside the guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Capability advertisement | Agent Cards describe identity, interfaces, skills, modalities, capabilities, security schemes, and extensions | Skill truthfulness, service quality, registry trust, and semantic compatibility |
| Black-box collaboration | Agents exchange messages and artifacts without exposing internal memory, tools, prompts, or reasoning | Verification of remote behavior, data use, intermediate actions, or artifact correctness |
| Task abstraction | Tasks have IDs, context, status, history, artifacts, continuation, cancellation, and interrupted states | Business-level success, compensation, durable workflow semantics, and guaranteed cancellation |
| Long-running work | Polling, SSE, subscriptions, and webhook push support disconnected execution | Complete delivery durability, replay policy, token lifetime, and recovery policy |
| Multimodal exchange | Unified Parts carry text, bytes, URLs, or structured data; artifacts package results | Safe file retrieval, schema meaning, content provenance, and data quality |
| Capability negotiation | Interface versions, bindings, extension URIs, input/output modes, and capability flags | Universal skill schemas, automatic semantic negotiation, and nonfragmented optional-feature support |
| Enterprise security design | HTTPS/TLS, declared authentication, OAuth PKCE and device flow, mTLS support, signed cards, tenant fields, caller-scoped task access | Complete identity, authorization, delegation provenance, revocation, prompt-injection defense, and behavioral trust |

### Capability discovery as a runtime contract

Traditional integration often starts with a hard-coded endpoint and an agreed API. A2A makes the remote agent’s capabilities discoverable at runtime. The client can fetch a card, match a skill to a goal, select a compatible interface, and determine whether streaming or push is available.

This is especially useful in an ecosystem where agents may be added, replaced, or operated by separate owners. A procurement orchestrator need not embed every supplier’s implementation details. It can route to an agent that advertises purchase-order handling, structured input, and the required authentication scheme.

The design is innovative in the context of current LLM systems because the advertised unit is an agent rather than a function. It also combines discovery with interaction modes and task capabilities. But it is not a guarantee of semantic interoperability. The core card contains descriptions, tags, examples, and modalities; it does not require a universal JSON Schema for every skill’s business input and output. One analysis specifically identifies this as a limitation of the core design. [A2A implementation and design analysis](https://codilime.com/blog/a2a-protocol-explained/)

Registries can improve search, ownership, health, and policy. They are not standardized by A2A itself, so organizations still need to agree on registry governance and freshness.

### Opaque agents as composable actors

A2A explicitly avoids requiring the remote agent to expose its internal state, tools, prompts, memory, model, or framework. This produces several practical benefits:

- a LangGraph agent can cooperate with a CrewAI agent;
- a Python service can call a Go service without importing its runtime;
- a vendor can expose a specialized capability without disclosing proprietary implementation;
- the remote owner can replace its model or internal tools while preserving the A2A interface;
- the calling agent can reason in terms of outcomes rather than implementation details.

This is different from exposing an internal function as a tool. A remote agent can ask questions, wait for authorization, produce several artifacts, and use its own judgment about execution.

Opacity is also a security and verification trade-off. The caller cannot automatically determine what the remote agent did with the delegated data, whether it used an approved tool, whether it retained credentials, or whether a returned artifact was generated from valid evidence. A2A protects implementation boundaries; it does not provide remote process transparency.

### Task-oriented interaction

The task model is a major departure from request/response-only integration. A2A gives long-running work a common shape:

- a unique task identity;
- a context for related exchanges;
- explicit progress and interruption;
- input-required and auth-required states;
- status and artifact events;
- cancellation requests;
- polling and subscriptions;
- push notifications;
- terminal outcomes.

That model fits work such as contract review, claims processing, supplier qualification, background checks, and research. These operations may involve human approvals, third-party APIs, queues, retries, or several subordinate agents.

It also gives observability systems a common vocabulary. An operator can record `SUBMITTED`, `WORKING`, `INPUT_REQUIRED`, `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELED`, and `REJECTED` regardless of the remote framework.

The limits are equally important. A task state says what the protocol knows about execution, not whether the business result is correct. `COMPLETED` means the agent reached a completed state and returned its protocol result; it does not mean that a contract interpretation is legally sound or that a purchase order should be approved. Cancellation is best effort. Task history may omit transient messages. Artifact mutation and version lineage are partly left to the client.

### Long-running work, streaming, and push

A2A treats asynchronous work as a first-class design concern rather than an add-on. SSE supports real-time progress and artifact chunks while the connection remains open. `SubscribeToTask` supports later observation. Webhooks support clients that disconnect, sleep, or operate in an event-driven environment.

This combination addresses a practical gap in ordinary API integration. A service can return a job ID, but every organization then invents its own job states, callback format, retry policy, and artifact retrieval convention. A2A supplies a common task and event vocabulary.

It does not make asynchronous delivery automatically reliable. The client must authenticate webhooks, deduplicate deliveries, verify task IDs, and decide how much state to persist. The server must defend against malicious webhook URLs, excessive retries, and resource exhaustion. A disconnected stream is not automatically a durable event log.

### Multimodal messages and artifacts

A2A’s `Part` structure allows a message or artifact to contain text, inline bytes, a URL reference, or structured data. A single task can therefore carry a user instruction, an image, a JSON form, and a generated document. Artifacts can be streamed in chunks and returned as files, reports, images, or machine-readable records.

This is useful for agents whose work product is not merely text:

- a claims agent can receive a scanned form and return extracted fields;
- a design agent can return an image and structured metadata;
- a procurement agent can return both a human-readable recommendation and a purchase-order object;
- a compliance agent can return a report and evidence references.

The protocol defines the container, not the meaning or trustworthiness of its content. A URL part can create SSRF risk. An image can contain malicious or misleading content. Structured JSON can be syntactically valid but semantically wrong. Content validation and provenance remain application responsibilities.

### Version and extension negotiation

A2A v1 improves compatibility by placing protocol versions on individual interfaces and using explicit service parameters. A client can select JSON-RPC v1.0 for one endpoint and gRPC v1.0 for another, or choose a v0.3 interface during migration if the card advertises it.

Versioned extension URIs provide a way to add domain-specific behavior without changing the core. A client can declare which extensions it wants to use, and an extension marked required can cause a clear failure if the server does not support it.

This is more disciplined than silently assuming that every implementation has the same optional feature set. It also introduces a compatibility burden: clients must understand whether an extension is optional, required, compatible with the selected binding, and safe to use with a particular tenant or skill.

### Enterprise-oriented security choices

The v1 release adds several enterprise-oriented mechanisms:

- signed Agent Cards using JCS and JWS;
- explicit interface-level protocol versions;
- mutual TLS support;
- OAuth authorization-code PKCE;
- OAuth device-code flow;
- removal of implicit and password flows;
- per-skill security declarations;
- tenant routing fields;
- caller-scoped task visibility;
- formal error mappings across bindings;
- production HTTPS and encrypted gRPC requirements.

These are meaningful design improvements. They reduce ambiguity and make common enterprise infrastructure easier to reuse. They do not mean that A2A itself enforces complete enterprise security.

The specification delegates important decisions to implementers: how a card signer is trusted, how an identity provider issues credentials, how a task is bound to a principal, how delegated authority propagates through several agents, how long a credential remains valid, how a webhook is allowlisted, and how prompt injection is detected.

### What the security evidence supports

The supplied independent security evidence argues for a careful interpretation of A2A’s security design.

A 2026 ACM comparison of A2A, ACP, and CORAL concludes that existing agent communication protocols remain insufficiently secure overall, although its abstract does not provide a separate A2A vulnerability count. [ACM comparative security analysis](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3803431)

A2ABreak, a 2026 specification-level preprint, models A2A as a finite-state system and reports 11 vulnerabilities under a full-compliance threat model. Its reported examples include cross-client context injection, loss of original identity across delegation hops, and unattested skill claims. The study does not test deployed implementations or transport-layer security, and its findings should therefore be read as protocol-design analysis rather than incident statistics. [A2ABreak analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.10871v1)

The context-injection concern follows from the difference between a task ID and a context ID. A task is accessed through authorization-scoped operations, but a context identifier can group accumulated history. If an implementation accepts a caller-supplied context without binding it to an owner, an authenticated caller who learns the identifier may be able to inject into or benefit from the wrong context. The official guidance requires authorization scoping for task operations, but deployments must also bind context ownership and access.

The multi-hop identity concern follows from transport-layer authentication. Agent A may authenticate to Agent B using Agent A’s identity, even when Agent A is acting for a user and delegating to Agent C. Unless a deployment adds a delegation token, chain-of-custody record, or equivalent mechanism, downstream agents know the immediate caller but not necessarily the original principal or the exact authority being delegated.

The skill-attestation concern follows from self-described Agent Cards. A signed card can establish that a recognized publisher signed a claim, but it does not prove that the skill is effective, safe, or appropriate for sensitive data. Organizations therefore need trusted registries, allowlists, certification, behavioral monitoring, or domain-specific attestation for high-impact workflows.

The research evidence does not justify calling these issues proof that every A2A deployment is insecure. It does justify rejecting the stronger marketing interpretation that protocol use alone creates trust.

### A misleading security result that should not be attributed to A2A

The supplied material includes an ACM record titled *Improving Google A2A Protocol: Protecting Sensitive Data and Mitigating Unintended Harms in Multi-Agent Systems*. Its fetched metadata gives a publication date of April 4, 2022, three years before Google announced A2A. The abstract reports a 5,000-trial interceptor evaluation and a 0% structural success rate under stated assumptions.

Because the date conflicts with A2A’s independently documented April 2025 introduction, the provenance of that record cannot be reconciled from the supplied evidence. The 5,000-trial result should not be cited as an empirical security result for A2A. [Conflicting ACM record](https://doi.org/10.1145/3821216)

## The specific problems A2A is designed to solve

A2A is best understood as a response to a set of integration problems created when agents become numerous, specialized, independently deployed, and organizationally separated.

| Problem | A2A mechanism | What it solves and what it does not |
|---|---|---|
| Fragmented agent ecosystem | Common data model, operations, bindings, and version signaling | Creates a shared communication contract; does not create a shared ontology or quality standard |
| Bespoke point-to-point integrations | Agent Cards and common task operations | Reduces custom connectors between compliant agents; does not eliminate registry, policy, or migration work |
| Vendor and framework incompatibility | Opaque HTTP/gRPC/REST interface | Allows different frameworks and languages to collaborate; does not guarantee equivalent behavior |
| Inability to discover remote capability | Agent Cards, skills, interfaces, modalities, and optional registries | Makes capability advertisement machine-readable; does not attest that claims are true |
| Inability to delegate across boundaries | Client/remote roles, `SendMessage`, `Task`, context and references | Gives delegation a standard shape; does not decide whether delegation is authorized |
| Long-running workflows | Task states, polling, SSE, subscriptions, artifacts, and push notifications | Handles waiting, interruption, disconnection, and progress; does not guarantee durable delivery or cancellation |
| Opaque-agent interoperability | Black-box collaboration through messages and artifacts | Protects implementation and intellectual property boundaries; limits behavioral verification |
| Rich or multimodal exchange | Parts and Artifacts | Carries text, files, bytes, URLs, and structured data; does not validate semantic correctness |
| Enterprise access concerns | HTTPS, declared schemes, OAuth improvements, mTLS, signed cards, tenant fields, scopes | Gives deployments standard hooks for identity and policy; leaves complete trust and authorization to implementers |
| Operational visibility | Explicit lifecycle, status events, list/get operations, formal errors | Makes cross-agent monitoring more consistent; does not create an audit system automatically |

### Fragmentation and the point-to-point integration burden

Before a common protocol, a multi-agent workflow often required a custom connector for each pairing. Every connector could have its own message format, authentication method, error model, callback convention, and task-state vocabulary. Adding one more agent multiplied maintenance rather than simply adding one more capability.

A travel planner illustrates the problem. One user request may require a flight agent, hotel agent, local-tour agent, and currency-advisory agent. Without a shared contract, the planner must know four proprietary APIs and coordinate four incompatible interaction models. The example is illustrative, but the engineering problem is real: bespoke links become harder to test, scale, and replace as the number of agents grows. [A2A integration problem](https://huggingface.co/blog/1bo/a2a-protocol-explained)

A2A reduces the burden by giving every participating agent the same broad vocabulary: discover the card, select an interface, send a message, receive a task or direct message, retrieve state, consume artifacts, and handle errors. A new compliant agent can fit the same orchestration pattern.

The mechanism does not eliminate all integration work. Teams still need to agree on business semantics, identifiers, data classification, compensation behavior, and authorization. A2A removes wire-level repetition; it does not remove domain-level contracts.

### Vendor and framework incompatibility

A2A is explicitly designed for agents built with different frameworks, languages, and deployment stacks. The remote agent is reached through the protocol rather than through an imported framework object or proprietary SDK.

The Google Cloud purchasing example places a LangGraph seller and a CrewAI seller behind A2A endpoints and lets a Google ADK concierge call both. A cross-language contract-compliance example uses a Python agent and a Go agent. These examples demonstrate the intended boundary: the caller needs a protocol client, not the implementation language or framework of the remote agent.

The limit is that syntactic interoperability does not imply behavioral interchangeability. Two agents can both advertise `contract-review` while using different definitions of material breach, different evidence requirements, or different output schemas. A2A can carry the exchange, but governance must define what the result means.

### Capability discovery and delegation

An orchestrator cannot delegate dynamically if it does not know which agents exist or what they can do. Hard-coded endpoints create a new integration project each time a provider changes.

Agent Cards solve the mechanical discovery problem. An orchestrator can retrieve a card, inspect skills and supported interfaces, check modalities, identify authentication requirements, and decide whether the agent is a candidate. The extended card can expose additional capabilities after authentication.

The mechanism is deliberately loose. A card advertises capabilities but does not force the client to use a particular skill identifier, and the core specification does not provide a universal skill-input schema or quality score. Discovery therefore enables selection, not proof. An enterprise may still require a trusted registry, signed cards, issuer pinning, certification, or a human approval step before sending sensitive data.

Delegation itself is represented by the message and task model. The client sends an outcome-oriented request, receives a task, and can observe or continue that task. A2A standardizes the handoff without requiring the remote agent to expose internal plans.

### Long-running and disconnected work

Many enterprise workflows do not fit a single request timeout. A supplier may need to confirm inventory; a claims agent may need to process several documents; a hiring workflow may wait for a human approval; a research agent may run for hours.

A2A addresses this with explicit state and several delivery options:

- polling works for simple clients;
- SSE provides immediate status and artifact updates;
- task subscription supports later observation;
- webhooks support disconnected clients;
- `INPUT_REQUIRED` and `AUTH_REQUIRED` represent pauses that are part of the workflow;
- artifacts separate concrete results from transient conversation.

This is more expressive than returning an opaque job ID and asking every client to invent its own status API. It also creates obligations. A deployment must decide how long tasks remain available, how webhook retries work, how credentials expire while a task is running, how canceled tasks interact with downstream side effects, and whether a returned artifact can be trusted.

### Opaque-agent interoperability

A2A is designed for the case in which the client cannot inspect the remote agent’s internal memory, tools, prompts, model, or reasoning. That solves two practical problems at once.

First, it enables collaboration across organizational boundaries. A supplier need not reveal its inventory system or fulfillment logic to a retailer. A payment processor need not expose its internal risk model to a support agent.

Second, it protects implementation independence. A team can replace its model, framework, or MCP toolset without forcing every caller to change, as long as the external A2A contract remains stable.

The cost is reduced transparency. A client cannot infer from an Agent Card whether a remote agent is actually using an approved tool, whether it stores the submitted document, or whether it fabricated an artifact. For high-impact actions, opaque execution must be paired with evidence requirements, audit trails, attestation, result verification, sandboxing, and human approval.

### Multimodal and structured exchange

A2A addresses the weakness of text-only message conventions by defining Parts that can carry text, files, references, and structured data. An artifact can contain a PDF, a JSON record, and a human-readable explanation without requiring three separate proprietary channels.

This is relevant to:

- onboarding, where an agent may return credentials, a badge PDF, and a confirmation record;
- insurance, where an agent receives forms and images and returns structured claim data;
- manufacturing, where an agent returns a purchase order and supporting supplier documents;
- research, where an agent returns a report and cited source references.

The protocol does not define the business meaning of the structured data. A JSON object with a field called `approved` does not prove that the approval was valid. It also does not make external URLs safe to fetch. The receiving agent must validate content, provenance, authorization, and side effects.

### Enterprise trust and access concerns

Cross-agent workflows create trust boundaries that local function calls do not. The caller must decide:

- Is this the intended agent?
- Is the endpoint operated by the claimed organization?
- Is this caller authorized to invoke this skill?
- Which user or tenant is represented?
- Can the remote agent access only the data necessary for this task?
- Can a delegated credential be reused for another task?
- How can a later audit reconstruct what happened?

A2A provides mechanisms that help answer parts of these questions:

- Agent Cards declare security schemes;
- HTTPS and TLS protect transport;
- OAuth PKCE and device flow improve common authorization paths;
- mTLS can authenticate service identities;
- signed cards can protect metadata provenance;
- per-skill scopes support finer authorization;
- tenant fields support shared endpoints;
- task visibility rules limit retrieval;
- structured errors and state updates improve operational records.

But the protocol does not answer the entire trust question. Identity providers issue credentials; gateways enforce policy; servers authorize actions; clients verify signatures; registries establish organizational trust; security systems monitor behavior; legal and compliance teams define acceptable risk.

The distinction can be stated simply:

- A2A standardizes how agents find, call, and monitor one another.
- Enterprise security must still decide which agents should be allowed to do what.

### Representative scenarios

#### Employee onboarding

An onboarding orchestrator discovers HR, IT, and facilities agents through their cards. It sends `createEmployee` to HR, `setupEmailAccount` and `orderHardware` to IT, and `assignDesk` and `generateBadge` to facilities. The specialist agents stream updates such as “Laptop shipped” and “Desk assigned,” then return artifacts such as a badge PDF and account confirmation.

This scenario demonstrates discovery, delegation, parallel tasks, streaming, and artifacts. It also shows why authorization matters: account credentials and employee data should not be treated as ordinary text, and a returned artifact should not automatically trigger privileged actions.

#### Supply chain

A retailer’s inventory agent uses MCP to query local stock. When it detects a shortage, it discovers the supplier’s fulfillment Agent Card and delegates a purchase order over A2A. The supplier agent uses its own MCP connections to inspect available inventory, lead time, contractual constraints, and shipping systems. It returns a proposed fulfillment artifact, which may require human approval before execution.

Here A2A addresses the organizational boundary; MCP addresses each participant’s internal systems. Neither protocol decides whether the purchase is commercially or legally acceptable.

#### Contract compliance

A Python extraction agent sends a contract artifact to a Go policy-validation agent over A2A. The validator returns structured findings and a report artifact. The caller does not need to know how the Go service stores policy or which model it uses.

The protocol reduces language and framework coupling, but the organizations still need to define the policy version, evidence format, and meaning of “compliant.”

#### KYC and financial services

An orchestrator delegates identity verification, credit checks, sanctions screening, and human approval to specialist agents. Each specialist uses MCP to access approved systems; A2A coordinates work across separate services and returns artifacts.

This is precisely where A2A’s `AUTH_REQUIRED` state and tenant-aware task visibility are useful, but also where delegated-authority and provenance risks are most serious. A completed task cannot by itself establish that the underlying identity evidence was authentic or that the agent had the right to use it.

## Practical judgment

A2A and MCP should not be selected as mutually exclusive alternatives.

Use MCP when one agent or LLM application needs controlled access to tools, resources, prompts, or data. Use A2A when an agent must delegate work to an independent agent across a service, team, cloud, vendor, or organizational boundary. Use both when each specialist has its own tools and the specialists must collaborate.

A2A’s genuine contribution is a common, task-oriented contract for discovering and coordinating opaque agents, including long-running and multimodal work. Its release history and governance have matured from a Google announcement into a foundation-backed standard, although adoption numbers remain self-reported and not directly comparable.

The protocol solves the coordination problem better than bespoke agent glue. It does not solve the trust problem by itself. Signed Agent Cards, OAuth improvements, mTLS, scopes, tenant routing, task visibility, input validation, monitoring, and audit trails are valuable foundations, but they must be combined with deployment-specific identity, authorization, provenance, semantic governance, and prompt-injection defenses. The most durable architecture is therefore layered: MCP downward to an agent’s tools and data, A2A sideways to other agents, and enterprise policy and governance across both.
